1.pericope_label: And I saw in the right hand of him that sat on the throne a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals.

schools.summary: Gill takes the position of the book. He refers back for the throne and for who it was that sat upon it, and notes that the one seated had the book in his right hand, or, as the Syriac and Arabic versions render it, at or upon his right hand, lying by or near it; though according to the seventh verse the book appears to have been in his right hand, as our version and others render it.

Henry says that hitherto the apostle had seen only the great God, the governor of all things, and is now favoured with a sight of the model and methods of his government, as they are all written down in a book which he holds in his hand, to be considered as shut up and sealed in the hand of God. The designs and methods of divine Providence towards the church and the world, Henry observes, are stated and fixed, resolved upon and agreed to, as that which is written in a book: the great design is laid, every part adjusted, all determined, and everything passed into decree and made a matter of record. The original and first draught of this book is the book of God's decrees, laid up in his own cabinet, in his eternal mind, but there is a transcript of so much as was necessary to be known in the book of the scriptures in general, in the prophetical part especially, and in this prophecy in particular. God holds this book in his right hand, Henry says, to declare the authority of the book and his readiness and resolution to execute all the contents thereof; and the book in the hand of God is shut up and sealed, known to none but himself till he allows it to be opened, for known unto God and to him alone are all his works from the beginning of the world, but it is his glory to conceal the matter as he pleases, the times and seasons and their great events being kept in his own hand and power. It is sealed with seven seals, which tells us with what inscrutable secrecy the counsels of God are laid, how impenetrable by the eye and intellect of the creature, and also points us to seven several parts of this book of God's counsels; each part seems to have its particular seal, and, when opened, discovers its proper events, and these seven parts are not unsealed and opened at once but successively, one scene of Providence introducing another and explaining it, till the whole mystery of God's counsel and conduct be finished in the world.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson describe the roll and weigh the interpretations. Barnes says the chapter introduces the disclosure of future events in a manner eminently fitted to impress the mind with a sense of the importance of the revelations about to be made, and that the design of the whole chapter is evidently to honour the Lamb of God by showing that the power was entrusted to him which was confided to no one else in heaven or earth, of disclosing what is to come. Nothing else, he says, would better illustrate this than the fact that he alone could break the mysterious seals which barred out the knowledge of the future from all created eyes, and nothing would be better adapted to impress it on the mind than the representation in this chapter: the exhibition of a mysterious book in the hand of God, the proclamation of the angel calling on any who could do it to open the book, the fact that no one in heaven or earth could do it, the tears shed by John when it was found that no one could, the assurance of one of the elders that the Lion of the tribe of Judah had power to do it, and the profound adoration of all in heaven and earth in view of that power. Ellicott would render it, and I saw on the right hand of Him that sitteth upon the throne a book written within and behind, fast sealed with seven seals: it is not in but on, since the roll lay on the open palm of the hand, and it lies on the open hand of the Throned One, for it was not His will that the book should be kept from any. It is written, not on the inside only as was the usual way, but, like the roll of the book which Ezekiel saw, within and without. Some have thought, Ellicott says, that there are two divisions of predictions, those written within the roll and those written on the outer side; this is merely fanciful, and the passage in Ezekiel which supplies a guidance to the meaning might have shown the erroneousness of the thought, since clearly the lamentation and mourning and woe inscribed all over Ezekiel's roll indicate the filling up of sorrows, and here the same overflowing writing indicates the completeness of the contents, there being no room for addition to that which was written therein. But what is meant by the book? Numberless interpretations have been offered, Ellicott says: it is the Old Testament; it is the whole Bible; it is the title-deed of man's inheritance; it is the book containing the sentence of judgment on the foes of the faith; it is the Apocalypse; it is part of the Apocalypse; it is the book of God's purposes and providence. There is a truth underlying most of these interpretations, but most of them narrow the force of the vision; if we say it is the book which unfolds the principles of God's government, in a wide sense the book of salvation, the interpretation of life which Christ alone can bestow, we shall include probably the practical truths which underlie each of these interpretations, for all, Old Testament and New, man's heritage and destiny, God's purposes and providence, are dark till He who is the Light unfolds those truths which shed a light on all. Such a book, Ellicott adds, becomes one which contains and interprets human history and claims the kingdoms of the earth for God; the aim of all literature has been said by a distinguished critic to be little more than the criticism of life, and the book which Christ unfolds is the key to the true meaning of life. Robertson notes that the preposition means upon rather than in, the open palm, and calls the language anthropomorphic and drawn from Ezekiel. The word for book is a diminutive no longer felt as such, and the description is of a roll, not a codex as some scholars think; usually these papyrus rolls were written only on the inside, but this one was so full of matter that it was written also on the back side, and so was an opisthograph like that in Ezekiel. There are many allegorical interpretations of this fact, Robertson says, which are all beside the point. The participle rendered sealed is from an old compound meaning to seal up, found only here in the New Testament, and the word for seal is used in various senses, of proof or authentication, of a signet-ring, of the impression made by the seal, and of the seals on books closing the book. A will in Roman law, he reports, bore the seven seals of the seven witnesses; but this sealed book of doom calls for no witnesses beyond God's own will, and Alford sees in the number seven merely the completeness of God's purposes.

Clarke and Wesley describe the ancient book and the sealing. Clarke says the book was written within and on the back side, that is, it was full of solemn contents within, but it was sealed, and on the back side was a superscription indicating its contents; it was a labelled book, or one written on each side of the skin, which was not usual. As seven is a number of perfection, Clarke says, it may mean that the book was so sealed that the seals could neither be counterfeited nor broken, that is, the matter of the book was so obscure and enigmatical, and the work it enjoined and the facts it predicted so difficult and stupendous, that they could neither be known nor performed by human wisdom or power. Wesley says the right hand is the emblem of God's all-ruling power, and that he held the book openly, in order to give it to him that was worthy. It is scarce needful to observe, Wesley adds, that there is not in heaven any real book of parchment or paper, nor does Christ really stand there in the shape of a lion or of a lamb, neither is there on earth any monstrous beast with seven heads and ten horns; but as there is upon earth something which in its kind answers such a representation, so there are in heaven divine counsels and transactions answerable to these figurative expressions. Writings serve to inform us of distant and of future things, and hence things which are yet to come are figuratively said to be written in God's book. A book written within and without means that no part of it was blank, but full of matter; and it was sealed with seven seals according to the seven principal parts contained in it, one on the outside of each. The usual books of the ancients, Wesley explains, were not like ours, but were volumes or long pieces of parchment rolled upon a long stick, as we frequently roll silks, and such was this represented, sealed with seven seals; not as if the apostle saw all the seals at once, for there were seven volumes wrapped up one within another, each of which was sealed, so that upon opening and unrolling the first, the second appeared to be sealed up till that was opened, and so on to the seventh.

Victorinus and Bede identify the book with Scripture and differ over which part. Victorinus says the book signifies the Old Testament, which has been given into the hands of our Lord Jesus Christ, who received from the Father judgment; and that to open the book is to overcome death for man. Bede says the vision represents the mysteries of holy Scripture, as laid open to us through the Incarnation of the Lord, and that its concordant unity contains, so to say, the Old Testament without and the New within. On the seals Bede allows two accounts, that the book was either covered by all the fulness of the hidden mysteries, or written as a roll by the direction of the sevenfold Spirit. He gathers the Old Testament witnesses to the same figure: this is the book which is closed both to the learned and the unlearned in Isaiah, but of which even there the opening is announced, that in that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book; and of this Ezekiel also says that a hand was sent to him in which was the roll of a book, and He opened it before him, and it was written within and without. Ezekiel added what John concealed, Bede notes, namely what was written in the book, that there was written therein lamentations, and a dirge, and woe; for the whole course of the Old and New Testament forewarns that sins are to be repented of, the kingdom of heaven to be sought, and the wailings of hell to be escaped.

debates: What the book is. Ellicott lists the answers offered, the Old Testament, the whole Bible, the title-deed of man's inheritance, the sentence of judgment on the foes of the faith, the Apocalypse or a part of it, and the book of God's purposes, and holds that most of them narrow the force of the vision, preferring the book which unfolds the principles of God's government; Victorinus gives the first of those answers plainly, that the book signifies the Old Testament; Bede makes it the mysteries of holy Scripture laid open through the Incarnation; Henry takes it for the book of God's decrees transcribed so far as men need to know.

What the writing on both sides means. Bede takes the two surfaces for the two the Old Testament without and the New within; Ellicott calls such a division merely fanciful and says the Ezekiel parallel shows that the overflowing writing indicates only the completeness of the contents; Robertson says the many allegorical interpretations of the fact are all beside the point, the roll being simply too full of matter for one side; Clarke supposes a labelled book with a superscription on the outside indicating its contents.

What the seven seals are for. Clarke takes seven for the number of perfection and makes the sealing a security, so that the seals could neither be counterfeited nor broken; Henry and Wesley both find seven parts of the book, each with its own seal, opened successively; Wesley describes seven volumes wrapped one within another; Robertson reports the Roman will sealed by seven witnesses but answers that this book calls for no witnesses beyond God's own will, citing Alford for taking the number as simple completeness.
outliers: Wesley alone warns against the picturing itself, insisting that there is no real book of parchment in heaven and that Christ does not stand there in the shape of a lion or a lamb, but that there are counsels in heaven answerable to these figurative expressions.

Ellicott alone turns the vision into a claim about literature, holding that if the aim of all writing is little more than the criticism of life, the book which Christ unfolds is the key to the true meaning of life.
themes: a book in the right hand
written within and on the backside
the seven parts of the book

2.pericope_label: And I saw a strong angel proclaiming with a loud voice, Who is worthy to open the book, and to loose the seals thereof? And no man in heaven, nor in earth, neither under the earth, was able to open the book, neither to look thereon. And I wept much, because no man was found worthy to open and to read the book, neither to look thereon.

schools.summary: Gill identifies the angel and the mourners. He says this was not the uncreated angel, Jesus Christ, for he is afterwards spoken of as the lion of the tribe of Judah and as the Lamb in the midst of the throne, but a created one; though who he was, whether Gabriel, as some say, because his name signifies the strong or mighty One of God, is not material to be known, since angels are said to be mighty and to excel in strength. He is called strong here, Gill says, chiefly with respect to his voice, which he by reason of his great strength exerted so loudly as to be heard by all the creatures in heaven and in earth and under the earth; and this was not John the Baptist, but if a minister of the Gospel, rather some one since. On the next verse Gill renders it no one in heaven, whether angels or the souls of departed saints, and says that neither the one nor the other know anything of what is to come until it is revealed to them. On the next verse he says the apostle wept not so much on his own account, as though he feared his curiosity would not be gratified and the strong desire answered which had been raised in him at the sight of the book and increased by the angel's proclamation, but for the sake of the church of God, whose representative he was, and to whom the knowledge of this book and of the things contained in it he judged must be very useful and profitable. The Ethiopic version, Gill notes, reads, and many wept, that is, many of those about the throne as well as John.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson explain the herald, the word worthy and the three regions. Barnes says the angel was endowed with great strength, as if such strength were necessary to enable him to utter the loud voice of the inquiry, and quotes the observation that Homer represents his heralds as powerful, robust men in order consistently to attribute to them deep-toned and powerful voices. The inquiry to be made was one of vast importance, to be made of all in heaven, all on earth and all under the earth, and hence an angel is introduced so mighty that his voice could be heard in all those distant worlds. He is introduced as appointed to this office rather than as self-moved, and the design is to impress the mind with a sense of the importance of the disclosures about to be made and at the same time with a sense of the impossibility of penetrating the future by any created power: that one of the highest angels should make such a proclamation would show its importance, and that such an one, by the mere act of making it, should practically confess his own inability, and consequently the inability of all of similar rank, would show that the revelations of the future were beyond mere created power. Worthy, Barnes says, means having a rank so exalted and attributes so comprehensive as to authorize and enable him to open the book: it would require moral qualities of an exalted character to justify a man in approaching the seat of the holy God to take the book from his hands, and an ability beyond that of any created being to penetrate the future and disclose the meaning of the symbols employed. On the next verse he notes that there is no limitation in the original to man, the idea being that there was no one in heaven, evidently alluding to the created beings there, who could open the volume; and he asks whether it is not taught here that angels cannot penetrate the future and disclose what is to come, their faculties being limited in this respect like those of man. Nor in earth means among all classes of men, sages, divines, prophets, philosophers; and neither under the earth points to the abodes of the dead, where Barnes asks whether there may not be an allusion to the supposed science of necromancy, and an assertion that even the dead cannot penetrate the future. In all these great realms no one advanced who was qualified for the office, and even if any had a rank and moral character which might have seemed to justify the effort, none had the power of reading what was recorded. Neither to look thereon means so to open the seals as to have a view of what was written; that it was not beyond their power merely to see the book is apparent, since John himself saw it in the hand of him that sat on the throne. On the next verse Barnes says there seems to have been a pause to see if there were any response to the proclamation, and, there being none, John gave way to his deep emotions in a flood of tears. The tears may be regarded as an illustration of two things which occur constantly in the minds of men: the strong desire to penetrate the future, to lift the mysterious veil, than which no more earnest efforts have been made by men, whether by dreams, omens, auguries, astrology, the flight of birds or necromancy; and the deep grief which men often experience when all efforts to penetrate the future fail and they feel that they are left completely in the dark, since nowhere does man find himself more fettered and limited in his powers than here, nor anywhere is there such an intense disproportion between his desires and his attainments. Ellicott would render it a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice, and warns that we must not let the word worthy pass as though it were simply equivalent to strong enough: it seems to imply moral fitness, which is the true strength in the heavenly world, and it was not lack of intellectual capacity so much as the taint of moral unworthiness which hindered the reading of the book. To commune with God, he says, there is need of no subtle thought, no foreign tongue, no newest philosophy, since the pure in heart shall see Him, and Fox and Bunyan can more truly make Him known than masters of sentences and angelic doctors; those who are willing to do God's will know of God's doctrine. This thought corresponds, too, with the stress laid in the next verse on the victory of Christ, for it is not simply as divine Son of God but also as victorious Saviour and King of His people that He opens the book, His worthiness having been established in conflict and temptation. On the next verse Ellicott renders it, no one was able, in the heaven, nor on the earth, nor under the earth, nor even to look thereon, since it is of more than mankind that the Apostle speaks. The looking on the book is usually understood of the look cast on the book of one who would read the contents, and if so the thought is that none could open, still less read, the roll; it may, however, be that all who attempted to take the book were unable to face the glory in which it lay, as when Christ revealed Himself to Saul he could not see for the glory of that light. On the next verse Ellicott says the Apostle is not ashamed to call attention to his tears, the pronoun being emphatic: it was not a failure of faith but the outburst of an earnest heart, to which the knowledge of God and the destinies of his fellowmen were very dear, and those who have longed to see the end of oppression, fraud and sorrow on the earth will understand these tears. He quotes the judgment that the words, I wept much, can only be understood by those who have lived in great catastrophes of the Church and entered with the fullest sympathy into her sufferings, and that without tears the Revelation was not written, neither can it without tears be understood. Robertson says a strong angel was needed whose call could reach to the farthest limits of the universe, and parses the present active participle of the verb to herald or preach. Worthy means worthy by rank and character as well as by ability, and is here like the word meaning capable or qualified; the articles refer back to the book and the seals of the first verse, and it is an inversion of order, since the loosing of the seals precedes the opening of the book. On the next verse he notes the three prepositions with their several cases, including the whole universe as in the second commandment, and that the manuscripts vary between continuative and disjunctive negatives; to look thereon means into the contents of the book, and the universe, Robertson says, declines the challenge. On the next verse he notes the imperfect active, picturesque and descriptive, I kept on weeping much, the natural tense in these vivid visions, and suggests that it was perhaps weeping aloud.

Clarke and Wesley take the herald, the classes and the tears. Clarke calls the angel one of the chief of the angelic host, proclaiming as the herald of God, and reverses the clauses to their natural order, to loose the seals that he may open the book; who can tell what this book contains, he asks, or open its mysteries, since we whose habitation is in the dust know nothing of such things, though we are determined to guess. On the next verse Clarke glosses the terms in turn: no person or being, in heaven among all the angels of God, nor in the earth, no human being, neither under the earth, no disembodied spirit nor any demon; neither angels, men, nor devils can fathom the decrees of God. Neither to look thereon, he adds, since none can look into it unless it be opened, and none can open it unless the seals be unloosed. On the next verse Clarke says the apostle wept because the world and the Church were likely to be deprived of the knowledge of the contents of the book. Wesley says the proclamation to every creature was too great for a man to make, and yet not becoming the Lamb himself, and was therefore made by an angel, and one of uncommon eminence. On the next verse he says none means no creature, no, not Mary herself, and that in heaven, or in earth, neither under the earth means none in the universe, these being the three great regions into which the whole creation is divided; to open the book is to declare the counsels of God, and to look thereon is so to understand any part of it. On the next verse Wesley says the weeping sprang from greatness of mind, and that the tenderness of heart which the apostle always had appeared more clearly now he was out of his own power: the Revelation was not written without tears, neither without tears will it be understood, and how far are they from the temper of John who inquire after anything rather than the contents of this book.

debates: What the word worthy means. Ellicott warns that it must not be let pass as though it meant merely strong enough, and takes it for moral fitness, which is the true strength in the heavenly world, holding that it was the taint of moral unworthiness rather than lack of intellectual capacity that hindered the reading; Robertson keeps both sides, worthy by rank and character as well as by ability; Barnes the same, requiring moral qualities to justify the approach and an ability beyond any created being to penetrate the future.

Who the strong angel is. Gill denies that it is the uncreated angel, since Christ is named separately, and also that it is John the Baptist, and holds the question whether it was Gabriel not material; Clarke calls him one of the chief of the angelic host; Barnes says he is introduced as appointed to the office rather than as self-moved, and finds in his own proclamation a confession of the inability of all his rank; Wesley reasons that the proclamation was too great for a man and not becoming the Lamb.

What being unable to look thereon means. Ellicott gives the usual account, of the look of one who would read the contents, and then offers another, that all who attempted to take the book were unable to face the glory in which it lay; Clarke says none can look into it unless it be opened; Wesley takes it of understanding any part of it; Barnes notes that merely seeing the book was not beyond their power, since John himself saw it.

Why the apostle wept. Gill makes the grief representative rather than personal, for the sake of the church whose representative John was; Barnes reads it as a specimen of the desire to pierce the future and of the grief when that desire fails; Clarke says he wept because the world and the Church were likely to be deprived of the knowledge of the book; Ellicott denies that it was any failure of faith and calls it the outburst of an earnest heart.
outliers: Ellicott alone sets the plain believer above the schools on the strength of this verse, holding that since worthiness is moral fitness, Fox and Bunyan can make God known more truly than masters of sentences and angelic doctors.

Robertson alone observes that the two clauses stand in inverted order, since the loosing of the seals must precede the opening of the book, a point Clarke quietly corrects in his paraphrase without remarking on it.
themes: open the book and loose the seals
in heaven, in earth, under the earth

5.pericope_label: And one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof.

schools.summary: Gill identifies the speaker by elimination. The Ethiopic version, he notes, reads, one of these elders, that is, one of the four and twenty elders round about the throne; and he refuses the several conjectures in turn. It is not the first of the four and twenty books of the Old Testament, nor the patriarch Jacob, on account of the prophecy concerning Shiloh, Judah's son; nor Moses, who spoke of the Messiah as the great prophet of the church; nor John the Baptist, who pointed out the Lamb of God. These, Gill says, are all fancies and conjectures. It was one of the members of the Christian church, who was near the throne of God, had communion with him and knowledge of his will, and who in this visionary way is represented as comforting John under his sorrow and concern and giving him information; and sometimes, Gill adds, persons of superior abilities may receive instruction from meaner persons, as did Apollos from Aquila and Priscilla.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson explain the speaker and the two titles. Barnes says no particular reason is assigned why this message was delivered by one of the elders rather than by an angel, but that if the elders were the representatives of the church there was a propriety in their addressing John in his trouble: though they were in heaven they were deeply interested in all that pertained to the welfare of the church, and they had been permitted to understand what was as yet unknown to him, that the power of opening the mysterious volume was entrusted particularly to the Messiah, so that having this knowledge they were prepared to comfort him with the hope that what was so mysterious would be made known. Weep not means that there is no occasion for tears, since the object so much desired can be obtained and there is one who can break those seals. On the title of Lion, Barnes says the appellation is not elsewhere given to the Messiah, but it is not difficult to see its propriety here: the lion is the king of beasts, the monarch of the forest, and thus becomes an emblem of one of kingly authority and of power, and it is because Christ has power to open the seals, as if he ruled over the universe and all events were under his control as the lion rules in the forest, that the name is here given him. He is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Barnes adds, doubtless with reference to the prophecy in the blessing of Jacob, that Judah is a lion's whelp, and from the fact that the Messiah was of that tribe. Ellicott would render it, and one from among the elders saith unto me, Weep not; behold, the Lion, which is of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, conquered so as to open the roll and the seven seals thereof. The position of the word conquered, he says, is emphatic and should receive greater prominence, the verse having been translated, Behold, one conquered, even the Lion; the right to open the roll is thus made to turn not merely on the divine Sonship of our Lord but upon His victory, since He conquered and so opens the secret purposes of God to His Church. The thought is exactly parallel with other scriptures which give emphasis to the work of redemption, for it is for the suffering of death that Christ is clothed with glory and honour, and Paul traces the exaltation of Christ as the outcome of His humiliation; thus Christ, who in conquest is seen to be the power of God, in revealing the true philosophy of history is seen to be the wisdom of God. The lion, Ellicott notes, was the ancient symbol of the tribe of Judah: Jacob described his son as a lion's whelp, and the standard of Judah in the Israelitish encampment is said to have been a lion, the symbol of strength, courage and sovereignty. The Lion is also the representative of the royal house of David, since Christ cometh of the seed of David and the prophets have described Him as the Branch which would spring from the ancient stock; but there seems also a reference to the deeper thought that He who is the Branch is also the Root, being the one who was David's Lord and the true source and ground of all power to David and David's tribe, and of all who looked to Him and not to themselves for strength. Robertson notes the construction, one from among the elders, and the dramatic vivid present of the verb saith, and takes the prohibition as, cease weeping. Satan is called a lion by Peter, he observes, but the metaphor belongs to Jesus also: Judah is called a lion in the blessing of Jacob, and Jesus as the greatest of the tribe of Judah is the Root of David, or the Branch from this root. The verb rendered hath overcome is a first aorist active indicative, did overcome, coming first in the sentence as the great historical fact of the victory of the Christ.

Clarke and Wesley take the titles and the prevailing. Clarke says the Lion of the tribe of Judah is Jesus Christ, who sprang from this tribe as his genealogy proves, and that there is an allusion here to the blessing of Jacob, that Judah is a lion's whelp; the lion was the emblem of this tribe and was supposed to have been embroidered on its ensigns. Christ was the root of David as to his divine nature, Clarke says, and a branch out of the stem of Jesse as to his human nature; he prevailed by the merit of his incarnation, passion and death, and to open the book is to explain and execute all the purposes and decrees of God in relation to the government of the world and the Church. Wesley says the elder was probably one of those who rose with Christ and afterwards ascended into heaven, perhaps one of the patriarchs, and that some think it was Jacob, from whose prophecy the name of Lion is given him. The Lion of the tribe of Judah, Wesley says, is the victorious prince who is, like a lion, able to tear all his enemies in pieces; the root of David means that as God he is the root and source of David's family; and to have prevailed to open the book is to have overcome all obstructions and obtained the honour to disclose the divine counsels.

debates: Who the elder was. Gill lists the conjectures, the first of the Old Testament books, the patriarch Jacob, Moses, John the Baptist, and sweeps them all away as fancies, holding him to be a member of the Christian church; Wesley entertains the very conjectures Gill dismisses, supposing one who rose with Christ, perhaps a patriarch, and reporting that some think it was Jacob; Barnes and Robertson both decline to assign any particular reason for an elder rather than an angel, Barnes adding that the elders as representatives of the church were fitly the comforters.

What the Root of David means. Clarke divides it between the natures, root as to the divine and branch out of the stem of Jesse as to the human; Wesley keeps only the first half, that as God he is the root and source of David's family; Ellicott takes it first of the royal house and the Branch of prophecy, but finds behind it the deeper thought that the Branch is also the Root, David's Lord and the ground of all power to David's tribe; Robertson simply pairs the root and the branch.

Where the weight of the verse falls. Ellicott says the position of the verb of conquest is emphatic and should be given greater prominence, so that the right to open the roll turns not merely on divine Sonship but on victory; Robertson reaches the same point from the word order alone, the aorist standing first as the great historical fact of the victory of the Christ; Clarke locates the prevailing in the merit of the incarnation, passion and death; Wesley in the overcoming of all obstructions.
outliers: Ellicott alone ends on an antithesis drawn from Paul, that Christ who in conquest is seen to be the power of God is, in revealing the true philosophy of history, seen to be the wisdom of God.

Gill alone turns the verse to a practical use about teachers and learners, observing from the elder's instructing the apostle that persons of superior abilities may receive instruction from meaner ones, as Apollos did from Aquila and Priscilla.
themes: the Lion of the tribe of Judah

6.pericope_label: And I beheld, and, lo, in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders, stood a Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent forth into all the earth.

schools.summary: Gill notes only that the words, in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, are left out in the Syriac version.

Henry says the apostle here beholds the book taken into the hands of the Lord Jesus Christ in order to its being unsealed and opened by him, and describes Christ by his place and station: in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts and of the elders. He was on the same throne with the Father, Henry says, and was nearer to him than either the elders or the ministers of the churches; Christ as man and Mediator is subordinate to God the Father but is nearer to him than all the creatures, for in him all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily. The ministers stand between God and the people, and Christ stands as the Mediator between God and both ministers and people. Then Christ is described by the form in which he appeared: before he is called a lion, and here he appears as a lamb slain, being a lion to conquer Satan and a lamb to satisfy the justice of God. He appears with the marks of his sufferings upon him, to show that he interceded in heaven in the virtue of his satisfaction; and he appears having seven horns and seven eyes, perfect power to execute all the will of God and perfect wisdom to understand it all and to do it in the most effectual manner, for he has the seven Spirits of God and has received the Holy Spirit without measure, in all perfection of light and life and power, by which he is able to teach and rule all parts of the earth.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson place the Lamb and gloss the symbols. Barnes says we are not to suppose that he was in the centre of the throne itself, but that he was a conspicuous object when the throne and the elders and the living beings were seen, so placed as to seem to be in the midst of that group. The appellation of Lamb is often given to the Messiah for two reasons, because the lamb was an emblem of innocence and because a lamb was commonly offered in sacrifice; and as it had been slain means having the appearance of having been slain, with some marks or indications about it, whether covered with blood or bearing mortal wounds. The great work which the Redeemer performed was thus represented to John in such a way that he at once recognised him and saw the reason why the office of breaking the seals was entrusted to him. It should be remarked, Barnes says, that this representation is merely symbolic, and we are not to suppose that the Redeemer really assumed this form or appears in this form in heaven; we should no more suppose that he appears literally as a lamb with numerous eyes and horns than that there is a literal throne and a sea of glass there, or seats and elders and crowns of gold. The seven horns are emblems of authority and power, for the horn is a symbol of power and dominion, and the propriety of this symbol is laid in the fact that the strength of an animal is in the horn and that it is by this that he obtains a victory over other animals; the number seven denotes completeness, so that he had so large a number as to denote complete dominion. The seven eyes are symbols of intelligence. Ellicott would render it, and I saw in the midst of the throne and of the four living beings, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb, or a little Lamb, standing as if having been slain. The position of the Lamb is described from the seer's point of view: the Lamb is not on the throne but in the middle front of it, and so apparently between the living creatures and in the midst of the circle formed by the twenty-four elders. The passage is most striking, Ellicott says: the Evangelist is told of the Lion which will open the seals, he looks, and lo, it is a Lamb, yes, a little Lamb, for the word is diminutive. There is deep significance in this; when we read of the Lion we think of power and majesty, and we are right, for all power in heaven and earth is Christ's, but it is power manifested in seeming weakness. The waters of Shiloah are mightier than the Euphrates; righteousness and purity, meekness and gentleness, are greater than carnal weapons; the Lamb is mightier than the roaring lion which goeth about seeking whom he may devour. But it is a Lamb as if it had been slain: the wound-marks are there, but it is not dead, it is standing, for it represents Him who though He died is alive for evermore; the signs of suffering and death are visible, for it is not the Lamb but the suffering Lamb which is exalted, not the Christ but the Christ crucified which is the power of God, the Christ lifted up from the earth who draws all men unto Him, the corn of wheat which dies and brings forth fruit. As such He is the worship of the Church and the world which He has redeemed. Robertson says the seer was stirred by the words of the elder, and grants that it is not quite clear where the Lamb was standing in the vision, whether close to the throne or in the space between the throne and the elders. Elsewhere in the New Testament a different word is used of Christ as Lamb, but in the Apocalypse this diminutive occurs for the crucified Christ twenty-nine times in twelve chapters. The participle rendered standing is a second perfect active, and the words as though it had been slain use the particle as if because the Lamb is now alive, but in appearance with the marks of the sacrifice; the Christ as the Lamb, Robertson adds, is both sacrifice and Priest. The horn is a common Old Testament symbol for strength and kingly power, and fulness of power is symbolized by seven; the seven eyes are like those in Zechariah and denote omniscience. Here they are identified with the seven Spirits of Christ, Robertson notes, while earlier in the book the seven Spirits are clearly the Holy Spirit of God, who blaze like torches and like the eyes of Christ: the Holy Spirit is both Spirit of God and of Christ.

Clarke and Wesley take the sacrifice and the sevenfold symbols. Clarke says the Lamb is Christ, so called because he was a sacrificial offering, and that the Greek word signifies a little or delicate lamb. As it had been slain means as if now in the act of being offered, and this is very remarkable, Clarke says: so important is the sacrificial offering of Christ in the sight of God that he is still represented as being in the very act of pouring out his blood for the offences of man. This gives great advantage to faith, since when any soul comes to the throne of grace he finds a sacrifice there provided for him to offer to God, so that all succeeding generations find they have the continual sacrifice ready and the newly-shed blood to offer. As the horn is the emblem of power and seven the number of perfection, the seven horns may denote the all-prevailing and infinite might of Jesus Christ, who can support all his friends, destroy all his enemies, and save to the uttermost all that come unto God through him. The seven eyes denote his infinite knowledge and wisdom, Clarke says, but as these seven eyes are said to be the seven Spirits of God they seem to denote rather his providence, in which he often employs the ministry of angels, and therefore these are said to be sent forth into all the earth. Wesley sets out three circles, Christ in or on the midst of the throne, the four living creatures making the inner circle round him, and the four and twenty elders making a larger circle round him and them. Standing means that he lieth no more, Wesley says: he no more falls on his face, the days of his weakness and mourning are ended, and he is now in a posture of readiness to execute all his offices of prophet, priest and king. As if he had been slain means doubtless with the prints of the wounds which he once received, and because he was slain he is worthy to open the book, to the joy of his own people and the terror of his enemies. The seven horns are, as a king, the emblem of perfect strength, and the seven eyes the emblem of perfect knowledge and wisdom, by which he accomplishes what is contained in the book, namely by his almighty and all-wise Spirit; and to these seven horns and seven eyes answer the seven seals and the sevenfold song of praise. The effectual working of the Spirit of God, Wesley adds, goes through the whole creation, and that in the natural as well as the spiritual world, for could mere matter act or move, could it gravitate or attract, just as much as it can think or speak.

debates: Where the Lamb stood. Barnes says he was not in the centre of the throne itself but seemed to be in the midst of the group made up of throne, living beings and elders; Ellicott places him in the middle front of the throne, between the living creatures and within the circle of the elders; Robertson grants that it is not quite clear; Henry takes him to be on the same throne with the Father, nearer to him than any creature; Wesley describes three concentric circles.

What follows from a Lamb appearing where a Lion was promised. Ellicott finds deep significance in it, that all power is Christ's but is manifested in seeming weakness, the waters of Shiloah being mightier than the Euphrates and the Lamb than the roaring lion; Henry states the contrast as a pair of offices, a lion to conquer Satan and a lamb to satisfy the justice of God; Clarke notes only that the word is a diminutive; Robertson counts its twenty-nine occurrences in the Apocalypse.

What the seven eyes are. Robertson calls them omniscience and then resolves the identification, since here they are the seven Spirits of Christ while earlier in the book the seven Spirits are the Holy Spirit of God, who is Spirit of both; Clarke starts from infinite knowledge but, because they are called the seven Spirits of God, moves to providence and the ministry of angels; Barnes calls them symbols of intelligence; Henry pairs them with the horns as perfect wisdom beside perfect power.
outliers: Barnes alone warns against pressing the picture, holding the representation merely symbolic and denying that the Redeemer appears literally as a lamb with many eyes and horns any more than there is a literal throne and sea of glass in heaven.

Wesley alone carries the reach of the Spirit into natural philosophy, arguing that the effectual working of the Spirit runs through the whole creation, since mere matter could no more gravitate or attract than it could think or speak.
themes: in the midst of the throne
a Lamb as it had been slain

7.pericope_label: And he came and took the book out of the right hand of him that sat upon the throne. And when he had taken the book, the four beasts and four and twenty elders fell down before the Lamb, having every one of them harps, and golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints.

schools.summary: Gill takes the approach and corrects a version. He came, Gill says, means that he drew nigh to the throne of God, engaged his heart to approach unto him, and came up even to his seat, which a mere creature, without a Mediator, cannot do. On the next verse he notes that the Vulgate Latin version reads, when he had opened the book, very wrongly, for the opening of it by unloosing the seals one after another is mentioned afterwards; what is meant here is that when it was observed that the Lamb took the book, and his commission to open, unseal and fulfil it, the adoration followed.

Henry says it is matter of joy to all the world to see that God deals with men in grace and mercy through the Redeemer, governing the world not merely as a Creator but as our Saviour. The harps were instruments of praise, he says, and the vials were full of odours, or incense, which signify the prayers of the saints: prayer and praise should always go together. Christ has redeemed his people from the bondage of sin, guilt and Satan, and has not only purchased liberty for them but the highest honour and preferment. What words, Henry asks, can more fully declare that Christ is, and ought to be, worshipped equally with the Father, by all creatures, to all eternity? Happy are those who shall adore and praise in heaven, and who shall for ever bless the Lamb who delivered them and set them apart for himself by his blood.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the difficulty, the tense and the vessels. Barnes says the Lamb took the book as if it pertained to him by virtue of rank or office, and raises a difficulty arising from the incongruity of what is said of a lamb, namely how a lamb could take the book from the hand of him who held it. To meet this, he says, several solutions have been proposed. Vitringa supposes that the Messiah appeared as a lamb only in some such sense as the four living beings resembled a lion, a calf and an eagle, that is, in respect to the head, while the body was that of a man, so that hands were attached to the front of the body by which he could take the book. There are great difficulties in this supposition, Barnes objects: besides that nothing of this kind is intimated by John, it is contrary to every appearance of probability that the Redeemer would be represented as a monster, since in his being represented as a lamb there is nothing that strikes the mind as inappropriate or unpleasant, but all this beauty and fitness of representation is destroyed if we think of him as having human hands proceeding from his breast or sides, or as blending the form of a man and an animal together. The representation of an unusual number of horns and eyes does not strike us as incongruous in the same sense, Barnes adds, for though the number is increased they are such as pertain properly to the animal to which they are attached. Another supposition, suggested by Professor Stuart, is that the form was changed and a human form resumed when the Saviour advanced to take the book and open it; this would relieve the whole difficulty, and the only objection to it is that John has not given any express notice of such a change. On the next verse Barnes says the acts of adoration described are emblematic of the honour done to the Redeemer by the church and by the course of providential events in the government of the world, and that falling down is the usual posture of profound worship, in which there was usually entire prostration on the earth. The construction and the propriety of the case, he says, demand that the elders had each one of them harps: the Greek participle more properly agrees with the word for elders and not with the word for living creatures; there is an incongruity in the representation that the living creatures, in the form of a lion, a calf, an eagle, should have harps and censers; and the song of praise that is sung is one properly applied to the elders as the representatives of the church and not to the living creatures, since it says, Thou hast redeemed us to God by thy blood. The harp was a well known instrument used in the service of God, and Josephus describes it as having ten strings and as struck with a key. The word vial, Barnes says, denoting with us a small slender bottle with a narrow neck, evidently does not express the idea here: the article referred to was used for offering incense and must have been a vessel with a large open mouth, so that the word bowl or goblet would better express the idea, and the Greek word occurs in the New Testament only in the Revelation and is uniformly rendered vial, though the idea is always that of a bowl or goblet. Ellicott would render it, and He came, and He has taken it out of the right hand of Him that sitteth upon the throne. There is a change of tense, came and has taken, which seems to be due to the rapt attention of the seer, whose narrative trembles with his own intensity of feeling: he wept a while ago, and now he need not weep, for the Lamb conquered, He came, He has taken the roll. He is the wisdom of the Church, Ellicott says, among all pre-eminent, in whom all things will be reconciled and the purpose and meaning of all life's mysteries and sorrows made plain. On the next verse he says it is not the Church alone which is interested in the revelation that will throw light on life's mysteries and the delay of the kingdom, since the whole creation groaneth, waiting for the reign of righteousness, and therefore the four living beings, who represent creation, join with the elders, who represent the Church, in the adoration of the Lamb who holds the secret of life's meaning in his hand. The vials, which seem to be censers as they hold the incense, and the harps, it is perhaps more natural to suppose, were in the hands of the four and twenty elders and not of the living creatures; and here we have the praises, represented by the harps, and the prayers, represented by the censers, of the world-wide and age-long Church of Christ. The comparison of prayer with incense is in strict accordance with Old Testament language, Ellicott notes, and the incense held a conspicuous place in the ritual of the Temple, the greatest care being taken in its composition and the same compound not to be used anywhere but in the sanctuary, precautions which suggest its typical character; the true odours are the heart-prayers of God's children. He quotes the saying that of the three sweet ingredient perfumes, namely petition, confession and thanksgiving, is the incense of prayer made, and that by the divine fire of love it ascends unto God, the heart and all with it, and that when the hearts of the saints unite in joint prayer the pillar of sweet smoke goes up the greater and the fuller; and he adds that every prayer which broke out in sob from an agonising heart, every sigh of the solitary and struggling Christian, every groan of those groping God-ward, mingles here with the songs of the happy and triumphant. Robertson notes the perfect active indicative of the verb to take, not used for the aorist as the verb came is, but a vivid dramatic picture of the actual scene, he has taken it. On the next verse he observes that John drops back to the narrative tense, merely when he took, and notes the like vivid variation of tenses elsewhere. The harp is the traditional instrument for psalmody, and the golden bowls are broad shallow saucers; the word for incense is from the verb to burn incense, and the relative means that these bowls of incense symbolize the prayers of the saints.

Clarke and Wesley take the taking and the incense. Clarke says this verse may be properly explained by the saying of John that no man hath seen God at any time, the only-begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him: with Jesus alone are all the counsels and mysteries of God. On the next verse Clarke says the whole Church of God, and all his children in heaven and earth, acknowledge that Jesus Christ is alone worthy and able to unfold and execute all the mysteries and counsels of God. There were harps and vials, he says, and each of the elders and living creatures had one. The frankincense and odours offered at the tabernacle were emblems of the prayers and praises of the Lord, and that prayers are compared to incense appears from the psalm, Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; hence, Clarke notes, the rabbinic saying that the odour of the prayers of the Israelites is equal to myrrh and frankincense, but on the Sabbath it is preferred to the scent of all kinds of perfumes. The words which are the prayers of saints, he adds, are to be understood as the words This is my body are understood, that is, this signifies or represents my body: these odours represent the prayers of the saints. Wesley says that here was the psalm's Ask of me fulfilled in the most glorious manner, and that the taking is one state of exaltation reaching from our Lord's ascension to his coming in glory, though this state admits of various degrees: at his ascension angels and principalities and powers were subjected to him, ten days after he received from the Father and sent the Holy Ghost, and now he took the book out of the right hand of him that sat upon the throne, who gave it him as a signal of his delivering to him all power in heaven and earth, and he received it in token of his being both able and willing to fulfil all that was written therein. On the next verse Wesley says that now homage is done to the Lamb by every creature, and that the four living creatures together with the elders make the beginning while afterward they make the conclusion. Having every one, he says, means the elders, not the living creatures; the harp was one of the chief instruments used for thanksgiving in the temple service, a fit emblem of the melody of their hearts; and the golden phials are cups or censers, full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints, not of the elders themselves but of the other saints still upon earth, whose prayers were thus emblematically represented in heaven.

debates: Who held the harps and vials. Barnes gives three reasons for the elders and not the living creatures, that the Greek participle agrees with the word for elders, that harps and censers are incongruous in creatures shaped as a lion and a calf and an eagle, and that the song which follows fits the elders as representatives of the redeemed church; Wesley says flatly the elders, not the living creatures; Ellicott thinks it perhaps more natural; Clarke divides them, holding that each of the elders and living creatures had one.

How a lamb could take the book. Barnes raises the difficulty and reports two answers, that the resemblance to a lamb held only of the head while the body was a man's and furnished with hands, which he refuses as making the Redeemer a monster, and that the form was changed and a human one resumed for the act, which he says would relieve the whole difficulty but for the absence of any express notice of such a change; the others pass the point without remark.

What the golden vials were. Barnes objects that the English word denotes a slender bottle with a narrow neck whereas the article must have had a large open mouth, so that bowl or goblet would be better; Robertson calls them broad shallow saucers; Wesley cups or censers; Ellicott censers, since they hold the incense.

Whose prayers the incense is. Wesley says they are not the prayers of the elders themselves but of the other saints still upon earth, emblematically represented in heaven; Ellicott makes them the prayers of the world-wide and age-long Church; Clarke guards the figure, that the odours represent the prayers as the bread represents the body; Henry pairs the harps and vials as praise and prayer, which should always go together.
outliers: Barnes alone treats the vision as a scene to be staged, asking how a lamb could physically take a book and weighing two proposed answers, though at the previous verse he had warned that the representation is merely symbolic.

Ellicott alone widens the prayers to take in the inarticulate, gathering every sob from an agonising heart and every sigh of the solitary and struggling Christian into the incense that mingles with the songs of the triumphant.
themes: he came and took the book
odours which are the prayers of saints
the elders and the living creatures

9.pericope_label: And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation; and hast made us unto our God kings and priests: and we shall reign on the earth.

schools.summary: Gill takes the newness and records a variant. They sung a new song, Gill says, upon a new occasion and subject, redemption by the blood of the Lamb and his worthiness to open the sealed book, and in distinction from the old song of Moses and the children of Israel at the Red sea; this was a most famous and excellent song, an unheard of one, and which none could learn or sing but the redeemed of the Lamb. On the next verse, where the text reads hast made us unto our God kings and priests, Gill notes that the Alexandrian copy, the Complutensian edition, and the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic versions read them instead of us.

Barnes and Robertson take the song, the ransom and the reign. Barnes says the song is new in the sense that it is consequent on redemption and is therefore distinguished from the songs sung in heaven before the work of redemption was consummated. We may suppose that songs of adoration have always been sung in heaven, he says, and we know that the praises of God were celebrated by the angelic choirs when the foundations of the earth were laid, but the song of redemption was a different song and is one that would never have been sung there if man had not fallen and if the Redeemer had not died; this song strikes notes which the other songs do not strike, and refers to glories of the divine character which but for the work of redemption would not have been brought into view. In this sense the song was new, Barnes adds, and it will continue to be new in the sense that it will be sung afresh as redeemed millions continue to ascend to heaven. The occasion or ground of the new song, he says, is that by his coming and death he had acquired a right to approach where no other one could approach and to do what no other one could do; the language for thou wast slain is such as would be appropriate to a lamb slain as a sacrifice, and the idea is that the fact that he was thus slain constituted the ground of his worthiness to open the book. It could not be meant that there was in him no other ground of worthiness, Barnes cautions, but that this was that which was most conspicuous. The word rendered redeemed means properly to purchase, to buy, and is thus employed to denote redemption because redemption was accomplished by the payment of a price; to God means that we become his and are to be henceforward regarded as such, and this is the true nature of redemption, that by the price paid we are rescued from the servitude of Satan and are henceforth to regard ourselves as belonging unto God. By thy blood, Barnes says, is such language as they use who believe in the doctrine of the atonement, and is such as would be used by them alone: it would not be employed by those who believe that Christ was a mere martyr, or that he lived and died merely as a teacher of morality; if he was truly an atoning sacrifice the language is full of meaning, and if not it has no significance and could not be understood. On the four terms Barnes grades the breadth. Kindred is literally of every tribe, and the word means properly a comparatively small division or class of people associated together, referring to a family or race having a common ancestor; the meaning is that the redeemed will have been taken from all such minor divisions of the human family, not only from the different nations but from the smaller divisions of those nations, which can only be true if the knowledge of the true religion is yet diffused among all of them. Tongue denotes a division larger than a tribe but smaller than a nation, since a nation may be made up of those who spoke many different languages, as the Assyrian, the Babylonian or the Roman; and the meaning is that no matter what language the component parts of the nations speak, the gospel will be conveyed to them and in their own tongue they will learn the wonderful works of God. People properly denotes a people considered as a mass, made up of smaller divisions, and is distinguished from another word commonly applied to a people, which is applied to a community of free citizens considered as on a level, without reference to any minor divisions; the words here would apply to an army considered as made up of regiments, to a mass-meeting made up of societies of different trades, to a nation made up of different associated communities. Nation is a word of still larger signification, the people in a still wider sense, a people or nation considered as distinct from all others, embracing all who come under one sovereignty or rule; the words here used by John would together denote nations of every kind, great and small, and the sense is that the blessings of redemption will be extended to all parts of the earth. On the reign Barnes says the idea clearly is, in accordance with what is so frequently said in the Scriptures, that the dominion on the earth will be given to the saints, that is, that there will be such a prevalence of true religion, and the redeemed will be so much in the ascendency, that the affairs of the nations will be in their hands: righteous men will hold the offices, will fill places of trust and responsibility, and will have a controlling voice in all that pertains to human affairs. It is not said that this will be a reign under the Saviour in a literal kingdom on the earth, Barnes insists, nor is it said that the saints will descend from heaven and occupy thrones of power under Christ as a visible king; the simple affirmation is that they will reign on the earth, and all that is necessary to be understood is that there will be such a prevalence of true religion on the earth that it will become a vast kingdom of holiness, and that instead of being in the minority the saints will everywhere have the ascendency. Robertson notes that they sing is the present active indicative of an old verb meaning to chant with lyrical emotion, and that a new song is a cognate accusative, called new because a fresh song for new mercies, here in praise of redemption to Christ, like the new name, the new Jerusalem, the new heaven and the new earth, and not the old song of creation to God. For thou wast slain is the second aorist passive; the verb rendered redeemed is used by Paul and Peter of our purchase from sin by Christ; unto God is a dative of advantage, and with thy blood an instrumental use of the preposition. The blood of Christ as the price of our redemption runs all through the Apocalypse, Robertson says, and this is the reason why Christ is worthy to take the book and open its seals, that is, worthy to receive adoration and worship as the Father does. On men of every he notes that there is no word for men or for some before the preposition in the Greek, and points to a like ellipsis elsewhere with a like grouping of words for all mankind, representatives of all races and nations. On the next verse he says the aorist madest is a prophetic use anticipating the final result, that a kingdom and priests is the correct text as in the first chapter, and that they reign is a present active indicative in a futuristic use, though some manuscripts have the future, shall reign.

Clarke and Wesley take the newness and the singers. Clarke says a new song is composed on the matters and blessings of the Gospel, which was just now opened on earth, but that new song may signify a most excellent song, and that by this the Gospel and its blessings are probably signified; the Gospel is called a new song in the psalm, and perhaps there is an allusion in the harps here to the psalm which says, I will sing a new song unto thee, O God, upon a psaltery and an instrument of ten strings, and the same form of speech is found in the prophet, who seems to have the Gospel dispensation particularly in view. On thou hast redeemed us to God out of every nation, Clarke says it appears that the living creatures and the elders represent the aggregate of the followers of God, or the Christian Church in all nations and among all kinds of people, and perhaps through the whole compass of time; and all these are said to be redeemed by Christ's blood, plainly showing that his life was a sacrificial offering for the sins of mankind. On the next verse Clarke refers kings and priests to the law and to Peter's epistle. Wesley says they sing a new song, one which neither they nor any other had sung before. On thou hast redeemed us he observes that the living creatures also were of the number of the redeemed, and that this does not so much refer to the act of redemption, which was long before, as to the fruit of it, and so more directly to those who had finished their course, who were redeemed from the earth; out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation means out of all mankind. On the next verse Wesley reads hast made them, the redeemed, and says that so they speak of themselves also in the third person, out of deep self-abasement. They shall reign over the earth, he says, means the new earth, and herewith agree the golden crowns of the elders; the reign of the saints in general follows under the trumpet of the seventh angel, particularly after the first resurrection, as also in eternity.

debates: What the new song is new against. Gill sets it in distinction from the old song of Moses at the Red sea; Robertson sets it against the old song of creation sung to God earlier in the vision and groups it with the new name, the new Jerusalem and the new heaven and earth; Barnes contrasts it with all the songs of adoration sung in heaven before redemption was consummated; Clarke suggests new may simply mean most excellent.

Whether the singers are themselves among the redeemed. Wesley infers from us that the living creatures also were of the number of the redeemed, but at the next verse reads them and takes the third person for deep self-abasement; Gill records the manuscripts and versions that read them for us without drawing a conclusion; Clarke takes the elders and living creatures together as the aggregate of the followers of God.

What reigning on the earth means. Barnes reads a prevalence of true religion so complete that righteous men hold the offices and the affairs of nations fall into their hands, and denies expressly that a literal kingdom under a visible king is affirmed; Wesley reads the new earth, the reign following under the seventh trumpet and particularly after the first resurrection; Robertson only notes that the present tense is futuristic and that some copies read the future outright.

How much weight the four terms carry. Barnes grades them as four widths, tribe within tongue within people within nation, and builds on the gradation an argument that the gospel must reach every minor division of the race; Wesley compresses all four to out of all mankind; Robertson treats the grouping as a set phrase for all mankind and notes only the missing noun before the preposition.
outliers: Barnes alone turns the phrase by thy blood into a doctrinal test, saying it is language that would be used only by those who believe in the atonement and would have no significance in the mouth of one who held Christ a mere martyr or a teacher of morality.

Barnes alone reads his own century's map into the four terms, illustrating them from the Gaelic, Celtic, Anglo-Saxon, Mongolian and African races and from the British nation with its Scottish, Irish and Hindustani parts.
themes: every kindred and tongue and people and nation
we shall reign on the earth

11.pericope_label: And I beheld, and I heard the voice of many angels round about the throne and the beasts and the elders: and the number of them was ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands of thousands; saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing.

schools.summary: Gill takes the angels and the loud voice. The voice of many angels, Gill says, means immaterial spirits, made by Christ and worshippers of him, ministering spirits to him and his, the holy and elect angels, who are confirmed in their state by Christ; these John beheld in a visionary way and heard the articulate sounds formed by them. There were many of them, and how many there are, or were here, cannot be said: we read of a multitude of the heavenly host that appeared at the incarnation of Christ, and of more than twelve legions of angels that Christ could have had of his Father for a word speaking at the time of his apprehension, who would have rescued him out of the hands of his enemies; yea, that company is innumerable. The Syriac version, Gill notes, reads as the voice of many waters. On the next verse he says the loud voice signifies their zeal, fervour and affection for Christ, and is meant to make a free, open and public acknowledgment of him, that all might hear of his worthiness and of the praise and glory due unto him.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the circle, the number and the doxology. Barnes says the inhabitants of heaven unite with the representatives of the redeemed church in ascribing honour to the Lamb of God, and that the design is to show that there is universal sympathy and harmony in heaven and that all worlds will unite in ascribing honour to him. Round about the throne and the beasts and the elders means in a circle or area beyond that which was occupied by the throne, the living creatures and the elders: they occupied the centre as it appeared to John, and this innumerable company of angels surrounded them. The angels are represented here, as they are everywhere in the Scriptures, as taking a deep interest in all that pertains to the redemption of men, so it is not surprising that they are described as uniting with the representatives of the church in rendering honour to the Lamb. Ten thousand times ten thousand is one hundred millions, Barnes says, a general term to denote either a countless number or an exceedingly great number, and we are not to suppose that it is to be taken literally; and thousands of thousands implies that the number before specified was not large enough to comprehend all, since besides the ten thousand times ten thousand there was a vast uncounted host which one could not attempt to enumerate. The language would seem to be taken from Daniel, thousand thousands ministered unto him and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. On the next verse Barnes says the idea is that the fact that he was slain, or made a sacrifice for sin, is the ground or reason for what is ascribed to him. To receive power means power or authority to rule over all things, and the meaning is that he was worthy that these things should be ascribed to him: a part of them were his in virtue of his very nature, as wisdom, glory, riches, and a part were conferred on him as the result of his work, as the mediatorial dominion over the universe. Riches means abundance, that whatever contributes to honour and glory and happiness should be conferred on him in abundance, since himself the original proprietor of all things it is fit that he should be recognised as such. Wisdom means that he should be esteemed as eminently wise, having ability to choose the best ends and the best means to accomplish them; the feeling referred to arises from the contemplation of the work of salvation as a work eminently characterised by wisdom, wisdom manifested in meeting the evils of the fall, in honouring the law, in showing that mercy is consistent with justice, and in adapting the whole plan to the character and wants of man. Strength means ability to accomplish his purposes, manifested in overcoming the great enemy of man, in his control of winds and storms and diseases and devils, in triumphing over death and in saving his people. Honour means that he should be esteemed and treated with honour for what he has done, and glory refers to a higher ascription of praise than honour: the one may refer to the honour we feel in our hearts, the other to the expression of that in the language of praise. Blessing means everything which would express the desire that he might be happy, honoured and adored, and the words express the wish that the universe would ascribe to the Redeemer all honour and that he might be everywhere loved and adored. Ellicott renders it, and I saw, and I heard a voice of many angels around the throne, and the living beings, and the elders; and the number of them was myriads of myriads, and thousands of thousands. The chorus of the redeemed is followed by a chorus of angels, he says, quoting that which is the highest act of love, towards whatever persons it was manifested, from whatever calamities it saved them, must be the highest manifestation of the divine character and will, and therefore must be the cause of delight to all creatures, fallen or unfallen; if the Revelation is true, there can be no breach in the sympathies of any part of God's voluntary and intelligent universe. It is needless to observe, Ellicott adds, that the numbers are not to be taken literally, since they are simply employed to express the countless throng of that innumerable company of angels which raised the song, and he quotes the poet's line about numbers without number. On the next verse he calls it the second chorus, the chorus of angels, and notes that the doxology is sevenfold; though sevenfold it does not interrupt the advance of praise noticed in the earlier doxologies, for in this chorus the redeemed do not take part. The definite article is prefixed to the word power only, whereas in the doxologies of the fourth and seventh chapters it stands before each word; this has led some to view the single article as prefixed to all that follows and to regard all the words as though they formed one word, but Ellicott asks whether it may not be used to give emphasis to the power, since none, above or below, was able, which is the same word as power here, to open the book, but the Lamb has conquered to open it, and the chorus proclaims the Lamb worthy of that power. Some have thought that the seven terms of the doxology refer to the seven seals which the Lamb is about to open, Ellicott says, but this seems strained: the notion of completeness is common to this sevenfold blessing and the seven seals, and this is the only connection between them. Robertson says a new feature is introduced by the outer and vaster circle of angels who catch up the new song of redemption in antiphonal singing, answering the song of the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders, and that some manuscripts read as if before voice. Ten thousand times ten thousand is literally myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, a mild inversion of the natural order, which is the regular order in an older apocalypse; Daniel has thousand thousands and countless myriads, and they are all efforts to express the innumerable hosts of the angels. On the next verse Robertson notes that worthy agrees in grammatical gender with lamb though some manuscripts have the masculine, and that there is a change to the third person, is, instead of the second, art. The point of the song is the same as that in the two previous verses but the language differs, and the repeated article, the lamb the slain, refers back. There is one article before power for all the seven grounds of praise, power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honour, glory and blessing, though one of them is masculine, in contrast with the separate article for each item in the fourth chapter, here grouping them all together into a heptad of praise.

Clarke and Wesley take the multitude and the sevenfold applause. Clarke says the angels also are represented as joining in the chorus with redeemed mortals, and that ten thousand times ten thousand means myriads of myriads and chiliads of chiliads, that is, an infinite or innumerable multitude, in reference to Daniel. On the next verse Clarke says Jesus Christ is worthy to take, that is, to have ascribed to him, power, which is omnipotence; riches, beneficence; wisdom, omniscience; strength, power in prevalent exercise; honour, the highest reputation for what he has done; glory, the praise due to such actions; and blessing, the thankful acknowledgments of the whole creation. Here are seven different species of praise, Clarke says, and this is exactly agreeable to the rabbinical forms which the author of this book keeps constantly in view, and he cites a Jewish book for a sevenfold ascription of glory, magnitude, might, the kingdom, the honour, the victory and the praise. Wesley says, And I saw, the many angels; and heard, the voice and the number of them; round about the elders, so forming the third circle. It is remarkable, Wesley says, that men are represented through this whole vision as nearer to God than any of the angels. And the number of them was at least two hundred millions, and two millions over, and yet these were but a part of the holy angels, for afterward John heard them all. On the next verse Wesley notes that the elders had said, Worthy art thou, because they were more nearly allied to him than the angels; and that this sevenfold applause answers the seven seals, of which the four former describe all visible, the latter all invisible, things made subject to the Lamb, and every one of these seven words bears a resemblance to the seal which it answers.

Cyril reckons the multitude of the angels against the multitude of men. When the Son of Man shall come in his glory, and all the angels with him, Cyril says, behold, O man, before what multitudes thou shalt come to judgment: every race of mankind will then be present. Reckon therefore how many are the Roman nation; reckon how many the barbarian tribes now living, and how many have died within the last hundred years; reckon how many nations have been buried during the last thousand years; reckon all from Adam to this day. Great indeed is the multitude, Cyril says, but yet it is little, for the angels are many more: they are the ninety and nine sheep, but mankind is the single one.
