For according to the extent of universal space must we reckon the number of its inhabitants: the whole earth is but as a point in the midst of the one heaven, and yet contains so great a multitude; what a multitude must the heaven which encircles it contain, and must not the heaven of heavens contain unimaginable numbers? And it is written, Cyril adds, thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.

debates: Whether the sevenfold doxology answers the seven seals. Ellicott raises the reading and rejects it as strained, allowing only that completeness is common to both; Wesley holds it outright, that the four former words describe all visible and the latter all invisible things and that every word bears a resemblance to the seal it answers. Both are in this catena, and neither knows he is being contradicted.

Where men stand relative to the angels. Wesley finds it remarkable that men are represented through the whole vision as nearer to God than any of the angels; Cyril argues from the extent of space that the angels far outnumber men, mankind being the single lost sheep to their ninety and nine; Barnes places the angels in a circle beyond the elders without comment on rank.

What the single definite article before power is doing. Ellicott notes that elsewhere the article stands before each word of a doxology and suggests it here gives emphasis to power, the same word used when none was found able to open the book; Robertson takes it as grouping all seven grounds together into one heptad of praise, against the separate articles of the earlier doxology.

How far the numbers are to be pressed. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all say expressly that they are not literal; Gill says only that how many cannot be said; Wesley nevertheless multiplies them out to at least two hundred millions and two millions over, and adds that these were but a part of the holy angels.
outliers: Wesley alone converts the figures into a total, then immediately undercuts his own total by saying the sum is only a part of the angels.

Cyril alone turns the census outward on the reader, ordering him to count the nations and the buried centuries before he stands among them at the judgment, so that the vision becomes an argument about the hearer's own smallness.

13.pericope_label: And every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them, heard I saying, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb for ever and ever. And the four beasts said, Amen. And the four and twenty elders fell down and worshipped him that liveth for ever and ever.

schools.summary: Gill takes the extent of the chorus and the Amen. Every creature which is in heaven, Gill says, means animate or inanimate, angels and the spirits of just men made perfect, sun, moon and stars, and the fowls of the air. On the next verse he says the four living creatures said Amen, giving their assent to what the angels and every creature said, and expressing their desires and wishes that so it might be, and also their faith that so it was and would be.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the universal chorus, the fourfold doxology and the closing silence. Barnes says the meaning is that all created things seemed to unite in rendering honour to him who sat on the throne and to the Lamb: in the previous verse a vast host of angels are designated as rendering praise as they stood round the area occupied by the throne, the elders and the living creatures, and here it is added that all who were in heaven united in this ascription. All the universe was heard by John ascribing praise to God, a voice from the heavens, from all parts of the earth, from under the earth and from the depths of the sea, as if the entire universe joined in the adoration. It is not necessary to press the language literally, Barnes says, and still less is it necessary to understand by it, as one commentator does, that the angels who presided over the earth, over the under-world and over the sea are intended; it is evidently popular language, and the sense is that John heard a universal ascription of praise, all worlds seeming to join in it, all the dwellers on the earth and under the earth and in the sea partaking of the spirit of heaven in rendering honour to the Redeemer. Under the earth is supposed to be inhabited by the shades of the dead, and such as are in the sea means all that dwell in the ocean. In the psalm, Barnes notes, dragons and all deeps, beasts and all cattle, creeping things and flying fowl are called on to praise the Lord, and there is no more incongruity or impropriety in one description than in the other: in the psalm the universe is called on to render praise, and in the passage before us it is described as actually doing it. The hills, the streams, the floods, the fowls of the air, the dwellers in the deep and the beasts that roam over the earth, the songsters in the grove and the insects that play in the sunbeam in fact declare the glory of their Creator, and it requires no very strong effort of the fancy to imagine the universe as sending up a constant voice of thanksgiving. There is a slight change in the words of the ascription from the previous verse, Barnes adds, but it is the same thing substantially. On the next verse he says the voice of universal praise came to the living creatures from abroad and they accorded with it and ascribed honour to God; the living creatures and the elders began the work of praise and it was proper that it should conclude with them, that is, they give the last and final response. The whole universe, therefore, is sublimely represented as in a state of profound adoration, waiting for the developments to follow on the opening of the mysterious volume: all feel an interest in it, all feel that the secret is with God, all feel that there is but one who can open this volume, and all gather around in the most reverential posture awaiting the disclosure of the great mystery. Ellicott calls this the third chorus, the chorus of the universe, and renders it, every creature which is in the heaven, and upon the earth, and beneath the earth, and upon the sea, and all the things that are in them, heard I saying, to him that sitteth upon the throne and to the Lamb be the blessing and the honour and the glory and the might, to the ages of the ages. The song of the redeemed, echoed by the hosts of angels, is now merged in the utterance of all, he says; the song of praise rises from all quarters and from all forms of creation, and the whole universe, animate and inanimate, joins in this glad acclaim. To limit it to either rational or animate creation is to enfeeble the climax which this third chorus forms to the two preceding ones, and is to denude the passage of its fulness and of its poetry. The Hebrew mind delighted in representing every bird and every grass-blade as joining in God's praise, Ellicott says, and mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars, beasts and all cattle, creeping things and flying fowl, as well as kings of the earth and all people, were called on to bless the name of the Lord; Christian poets have told us that earth with her thousand voices praises God, and he quotes at length a hymn calling on nature to join every living soul beneath the spacious temple of the sky in one general song. The apostle who pictured all creation as waiting in eager expectation for the full redemption looked forward to the time when the whole universe, whether animate or inanimate, would bend the knee in homage and raise its voice in praise. The doxology which thus rises from the universe is appropriately fourfold, Ellicott notes, and the definite article, omitted in the English version, must be supplied before each word. The two preceding songs were in honour of the Lamb; in this last the praise is addressed to the Throned One and to the Lamb, and this linking of the Lamb with God as the Throned One is common throughout the book: here they are linked in praise, later they are linked in wrath, later in ministering consolation, later in triumph, and in the final vision the Lord God and the Lamb are the temple and the light, the refreshment and sovereignty, of the celestial city. On the next verse Ellicott reads, and the four living beings said, Amen, and the elders, omitting four and twenty, fell down and worshipped; the remaining words of this verse are wanting in some of the best manuscripts, he says, and they spoil the graphic force of the description. The Amen rises from universal nature and the Church of Christ falls down in silent adoration; thought and feeling assert themselves above all language. There are times when silence is the most eloquent applause, Ellicott says, and there are times when it is also the most real worship, and he quotes a wise precept of an old divine, let thy prayers be without words, rather than thy words without prayer, together with an English and an Italian poet who have given expression to the same feeling of the weakness of words, the one crying how feeble and how faint is speech to give conception birth and the other taking refuge in expressive silence. Here the inspired seer describes the chorus of praise as dying into a silence born of awe and gratefulness and love. Robertson says every created thing means every creature in a still wider antiphonal circle beyond the circle of angels, from all the four great fields of life, in heaven, upon the earth, under the earth, with upon the sea added, and no created thing is left out. This universal chorus of praise to Christ from all created life reminds one of the profound mystical passage concerning the sympathetic agony of creation in hope of freedom from the bondage of corruption, Robertson says: if the trail of the serpent is on all creation, it will be ultimately thrown off. The participle saying is masculine, a construction according to sense personifying the created things, though some manuscripts have the grammatical gender. Praise and worship are rendered to the Lamb precisely as to God on the throne, he notes, and there are separate articles here in the doxology as in the fourth chapter, with active power in place of the reserve of strength used in the angels' song. On the next verse Robertson says the four living creatures give their approval to the doxology after the antiphonal songs, and that they fell down and worshipped in silent adoration that closes the whole service of praise to the One upon the throne and to the Lamb; as in the fourth chapter, so here the representatives of the redeemed bow in silent worship. A Roman writer says that the Christians sing a song to Christ as to God, Robertson adds, and he is here worshipped by the universe.

Clarke and Wesley take the personification, the fourfold word and the text. Clarke says all parts of the creation, animate and inanimate, are represented here by that figure of speech called personification as giving praise to the Lord Jesus, because by him all things were created. We find the whole creation gives precisely the same praise, and in the same terms, to Jesus Christ, who is undoubtedly meant here by the Lamb just slain, as they give to God who sits upon the throne; now if Jesus Christ were not properly God this would be idolatry, Clarke argues, as it would be giving to the creature what belongs to the Creator. On the next verse Clarke says the four living creatures acknowledged that what was attributed to Christ was his due, and that the word twenty-four is wanting in the most eminent manuscripts and versions. Fell down and worshipped means fell down on their knees and then prostrated themselves before the throne, Clarke explains: this is the eastern method of adoration, first the person worshipping fell down on his knees, and then, bowing down, touched the earth with his forehead, and this latter act was prostration. The clause him that liveth for ever is wanting in three uncials, thirty-seven other manuscripts, the Syriac, Arabic, Coptic, Ethiopic, some copies of the Slavonic, the Itala and the Vulgate, and in two ancient commentators on this book; it is also wanting in some editions and is undoubtedly spurious, and a recent editor has left this and the above twenty-four out of the text. Now follow the least intelligible parts of this mysterious book, Clarke says, on which so much has been written, and so much in vain. It is natural for man to desire to be wise, and the more difficult the subject the more it is studied, and the hope of finding out something by which the world and the Church might be profited has caused the most eminently learned men to employ their talents and consume their time on these abstruse prophecies. But of what use has all this learned and well-meant labour been to mankind? Can hypothesis explain prophecy, and conjecture find a basis on which faith can rest? And what have we better in all attempts hitherto made to explain the mysteries of this book? Wesley says every creature means in the whole universe, good or bad, and that with the four regions of the world, in the heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea, agrees the fourfold word of praise: what is in heaven says blessing, what is on earth honour, what is under the earth glory, what is on the sea strength. This praise from all creatures begins before the opening of the first seal, Wesley says, but it continues from that time to eternity, according to the capacity of each; his enemies must acknowledge his glory, but those in heaven say, Blessed be God and the Lamb. This royal manifesto is as it were a proclamation, showing how Christ fulfils all things and every knee bows to him, not only on earth but also in heaven and under the earth. This book exhausts all things, Wesley adds, and is suitable to an heart enlarged as the sand of the sea; it inspires the attentive and intelligent reader with such a magnanimity that he accounts nothing in this world great, no, not the whole frame of visible nature, compared to the immense greatness of what he is here called to behold. On the next verse he notes that John has in view, through the whole following vision, what he has been now describing, namely the four living creatures, the elders, the angels, and all creatures, looking together at the opening of the seven seals.

debates: How literally the universal chorus is to be taken. Barnes says it is not necessary to press the language literally and rejects the reading that makes it the angels presiding over earth, under-world and sea, calling it evidently popular language; Clarke names the figure as personification; Ellicott insists that to limit it to the rational or animate creation enfeebles the climax and denudes the passage of its poetry; Robertson takes it flatly, that no created thing is left out.

Whether the fourfold doxology maps onto anything. Wesley assigns each of the four words to one of the four regions, blessing to heaven, honour to earth, glory to under the earth and strength to the sea; Ellicott says only that the doxology is appropriately fourfold and that the article must be supplied before each word; Robertson notes the separate articles and the substitution of active power for the reserve of strength in the angels' song, without pairing word to region.

What the closing prostration means. Ellicott makes it a silence born of awe and gratefulness and love, in which thought and feeling assert themselves above all language; Robertson calls it silent adoration closing the whole service; Barnes reads it as the universe waiting in reverential posture for the opening of the volume; Clarke describes the physical act instead, the kneeling and then the touching of the forehead to the earth.

What the closing words of the verse are worth. Clarke reports that four and twenty and the clause about him that liveth for ever are wanting in the most eminent manuscripts, versions and ancient commentators, and calls the latter undoubtedly spurious; Ellicott independently agrees they are wanting in some of the best manuscripts and adds that they spoil the graphic force of the description; Gill, Barnes and Wesley comment on the received text without raising the question.
outliers: Clarke alone breaks off at the end of the chapter to protest against the whole enterprise he is engaged in, asking what use all the learned labour spent on the least intelligible parts of this book has been to mankind, and whether hypothesis can explain prophecy or conjecture give faith a basis to rest on.

Clarke alone turns the universal chorus into a proof of deity, arguing that since creation gives the Lamb precisely the praise it gives the Throned One, the scene would be idolatry if Christ were not properly God.

Wesley alone reads the passage as a measure of the reader, saying the book is suited to a heart enlarged as the sand of the sea and leaves the attentive reader accounting nothing in this world great, not even the whole frame of visible nature.
